topics.title: Cauvery Water Dispute
bullets: On 30 July 2026, the CWMA upheld an order directing Karnataka to release 3,500 cusecs daily to Tamil Nadu for 15 days.
Karnataka had argued it faced an acute hydrological crisis with inflows 65.65% below the 30-year average due to Super El Niño.
Karnataka will challenge the order and has called an all-party meeting on 2 August 2026 to decide its next step. Background –
The Cauvery River originates at Talakaveri in Karnataka's Kodagu district and flows through Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Puducherry into the Bay of Bengal.
It is approximately 800 km long with a basin area of 81,155 sq km, making it one of India's most important inter-State rivers.
The basin is a lifeline for millions of farmers across the four States, and disputes over water sharing often trigger severe political and social tensions.
The dispute arises from competing demands: Tamil Nadu relies on Cauvery water for its delta districts, while Karnataka needs it for irrigation and Bengaluru's drinking water.
The basin's annual yield is estimated at 740 TMC, and its allocation has been contested for over a century.
Karnataka is increasingly focused on long-range water storage and diversion projects to secure its share.
The first formal agreement on Cauvery water sharing was signed between the Madras Presidency and the princely state of Mysore on 18 February 1892 .

The agreement established a framework for consultation and dispute settlement, requiring Mysore to obtain Madras's consent before building any new irrigation reservoirs on the Cauvery and its major tributaries .
The 1892 Agreement proved unsatisfactory to both parties, with Mysore feeling its development was being constrained and Madras feeling its prescriptive rights were not adequately protected .
The dispute escalated in 1910 when Mysore proposed the Kannambadi (Krishna Raja Sagara) reservoir, leading to arbitration and eventually the 1924 Agreement signed on 18 February 1924 .
The 1924 Agreement allowed Mysore to construct the Krishna Raja Sagara (KRS) dam with a capacity of 44.827 TMC and Madras to construct the Mettur Dam with a capacity of 93.50 TMC .
The agreement was intended to last for 50 years and expired in 1974, after which new negotiations became necessary .
After the 1956 reorganisation of States, the Cauvery basin was divided among Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Puducherry.
The dispute remained unresolved through the 1970s and 1980s, with a draft agreement in 1975 ultimately not adopted.
In 1986, farmers from Tamil Nadu petitioned the Supreme Court, leading to the constitution of the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (CWDT) in June 1990. Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal –
The CWDT was constituted in June 1990 under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, to adjudicate the disputes among the basin States .
In 1991, the Tribunal issued an interim award directing Karnataka to release water to Tamil Nadu in a stipulated pattern, leading to protests and an ordinance by the Karnataka government .
The matter was referred to the Supreme Court under Article 143, which upheld the interim award and denounced the ordinance, marking a significant judicial intervention .
After nearly 17 years of proceedings, the CWDT delivered its final award on 5 February 2007 .
The Tribunal allocated the annual yield of 740 TMC as follows: Karnataka – 270 TMC, Tamil Nadu – 419 TMC, Kerala – 30 TMC, Puducherry – 7 TMC .
The award specified that Karnataka must release 205 TMC of water to Tamil Nadu annually at the inter-State border point of Biligundlu . SC Judgment –
On 16 February 2018, a Supreme Court Bench delivered its landmark judgment on appeals filed by Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
The Court reduced Tamil Nadu's allocation and granted an additional 14.75 TMC to Karnataka, bringing its total share to 284.75 TMC.
It held that "drinking water requirement… has to be placed on a higher pedestal" and allowed 4.75 TMC to Karnataka for Bengaluru's needs.
The Supreme Court reduced Tamil Nadu's allocation from 419 TMC to 404.25 TMC and directed Karnataka to release 177.25 TMC of water to Tamil Nadu annually at Biligundlu .
The reduction was based on: 10 TMC on account of groundwater availability in Tamil Nadu's delta areas, and 4.75 TMC for Bengaluru's drinking water needs .
The Court emphasised that inter-State rivers are national assets and that no single riparian State can claim full rights over them .
The Supreme Court endorsed the Tribunal's monthly release schedule, which would continue for 15 years (until 2033) .
The monthly releases are designed to ensure that Tamil Nadu receives its share of water during the critical agricultural seasons.
The Court also directed the Central Government to frame a scheme for the implementation of the judgment within six weeks, leading to the constitution of the CWMA and CWRC . Legal Framework –
Article 262(1) empowers Parliament to provide for the adjudication of disputes relating to the use, distribution, or control of waters of any inter-State river or river valley .
Article 262(2) empowers Parliament to provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of such disputes .
This constitutional provision forms the basis for the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, and has been upheld as constitutionally valid by the Supreme Court .
The Act was enacted to provide for the adjudication of disputes relating to waters of inter-State rivers and river valleys.
Section 3 allows any State Government to request the Central Government to refer a water dispute to a Tribunal for adjudication .
Section 4 provides for the constitution of a Tribunal consisting of a Chairman and two other members nominated by the Chief Justice of India .

Section 11 of the Act states that "neither the Supreme Court nor any other Court shall have or exercise jurisdiction in respect of any water dispute which may be referred to a Tribunal under this Act" .
This is a direct implementation of Article 262(2) and ensures that water disputes are adjudicated by specialised Tribunals rather than the courts .
The Supreme Court has held that Article 131 (original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court) must be construed subject to the provisions of Article 262 .
The CWMA is the apex body responsible for overseeing the implementation of the Supreme Court's verdict on the Cauvery water- sharing dispute .
It is a statutory body that monitors the release of water by the upper riparian States and ensures compliance with the Supreme Court's directions .
The CWMA has the authority to hear appeals against orders of the CWRC and to issue directions to the basin States .
The CWRC is a subordinate body under the CWMA that functions within its ambit and is responsible for the day-to-day regulation of water releases .
It issues orders directing Karnataka to release water at specified rates during distress periods .
The CWRC's orders are subject to review by the CWMA, and States can appeal against them . Distress-Sharing Formula –
The distress-sharing formula is a mechanism designed to ensure equitable sharing of water during years of deficient rainfall .
Under the formula, when rainfall and reservoir inflows are below normal, the burden of shortage is shared between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu .
Tamil Nadu had urged the CWMA to apply the distress-sharing formula, seeking 9.45 TMC over 15 days (7,000 cusecs daily) from Karnataka .
The formula considers the actual inflows, reservoir storage levels, and the deficit from the normal flow in the basin .
When a deficit is identified, the CWRC and CWMA determine the quantity of water to be released to ensure that both States share the distress proportionately .
Karnataka, however, argued that the formula cannot be applied in the current year due to the unprecedented 65.65% deficit in inflows, which it attributed to Super El Niño . Recent News –
On 28 July 2026, the CWRC ordered Karnataka to ensure a flow of 3,500 cusecs of Cauvery water at Biligundlu for 15 days from 29 July 2026 .
Tamil Nadu had argued that it had received only 3.543 TMC of water between June 1 and July 26 against the quantity due, leaving a cumulative deficit of 35.391 TMC .
The CWRC decided to hold its next meeting on 11 August 2026 to review the situation .
Karnataka challenged the CWRC order before the CWMA at its 54th meeting on 30 July 2026, arguing that it was facing an acute hydrological crisis .

The State informed the Authority that cumulative inflows into its four reservoirs were 65.65% below the 30-year average and that it had only 3.55 TMC of water flow during June-July this year, compared to 116.92 TMC during the same period in 2025 .
Karnataka argued that releasing 3,500 cusecs would require it to release nearly 7,000 cusecs from its reservoirs due to transmission losses on the dry riverbed .
The CWMA upheld the CWRC's order, rejecting Karnataka's plea for a two-week abeyance of the order .
The Authority observed that inflows into Karnataka's reservoirs had improved, with the Kabini reservoir nearing full capacity and projected inflows of at least 15 TMC over the next 15 days .
The CWMA concluded that releasing 4.5 TMC (equivalent to 15 days at 3,500 cusecs) to Tamil Nadu would not affect Karnataka's drinking water requirements .
Tamil Nadu urged the CWMA to direct Karnataka to release 9.45 TMC over 15 days (7,000 cusecs daily) under the distress- sharing formula .
The State argued that the prevailing hydrological conditions justified a larger release to meet downstream requirements .
Tamil Nadu also pointed to low storage at the Mettur reservoir, which stood at 36.272 TMC on July 27, with an inflow of only 42 cusecs .
Karnataka argued that Tamil Nadu enjoys a "dual advantage" : it receives water from Karnataka during the southwest monsoon, while also benefiting from the northeast monsoon later in the year .
Karnataka also contended that Tamil Nadu already has substantial carryover storage from water released earlier .
Historical data shows that during distress years, the northeast monsoon has significantly augmented Tamil Nadu's reservoir levels .
Karnataka submitted that it needs to conserve at least 40 TMC of water to meet drinking water requirements until June 2027 .
The State warned that releasing water at this stage could affect both irrigation and drinking water needs in Karnataka .
The CWMA, however, concluded that releasing 4.5 TMC would not affect Karnataka's drinking water requirements .
Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar said the state would appeal against the order after consultations with ministers, officials, and legal experts .
He also convened an all-party meeting in Bengaluru on Sunday, 2 August 2026, to deliberate on the issue and formulate the state's response .
The meeting will be attended by former chief ministers, MPs, and MLAs representing the Cauvery basin region .

topics.title: BCI Inspection
bullets: The Bar Council of India (BCI) has directed all universities to conduct physical inspections of every affiliated and constituent law college within six weeks .
The move follows strong oral observations by the Supreme Court in July 2026 regarding the quality of legal education and the continued operation of deficient law colleges .
The BCI has also ordered an end to impermissible weekend, evening, and shift-based law programmes that dilute the mandatory character of a regular law course . Background –
The Bar Council of India (BCI) is the apex statutory regulator of the legal profession and legal education in India .
It was established under the Advocates Act, 1961, and has the authority to regulate legal education, grant recognition to law colleges, and enrol advocates .
The BCI frames the Rules of Legal Education, which prescribe minimum standards for infrastructure, faculty, and teaching hours .
The BCI is responsible for regulating legal education and maintaining standards of teaching, examination, and research in law colleges .
It grants recognition to law colleges and enrols advocates after they pass the All India Bar Examination .
The Council also plays a role in disciplining advocates and protecting the dignity and integrity of the legal profession .
The BCI consists of the Attorney General of India and the Solicitor General of India as ex officio members, along with one elected member from each State Bar Council .
The Council is headed by a Chairman, elected from among its members, and has a Vice-Chairman as well.
The BCI also has a Standing Committee on Legal Education, which oversees legal education matters and is chaired by a retired High Court judge .
Chairman of BCI is Senior Advocate and Member of Parliament (Rajya Sabha) Manan Kumar Mishra.
The BCI has repeatedly expressed concern over what it describes as a steady decline in the quality of legal education in India .
The regulator blamed it on the indiscriminate grant of No Objection Certificates (NOCs) by State governments and affiliations by universities, often without adequate scrutiny .
The Council has highlighted an acute shortage of qualified law teachers, stating that 40-50% of faculty positions remain vacant in more than 60% of government law colleges .
Many institutions rely on part-time or visiting faculty, which cannot replace the mandatory full-time core faculty prescribed under the Rules of Legal Education .
This shortage directly affects the quality of instruction, research, and practical training imparted to law students.
The BCI has pointed to inadequate libraries, moot courts, and research facilities, along with weak academic oversight, as factors contributing to the decline in educational standards .
Many law colleges operate with insufficient classrooms, poor library resources, and lack of legal databases .
The absence of proper moot court halls, legal aid clinics, and sports facilities further undermines the quality of legal education .
The BCI has expressed concern over the commercialisation of legal education, where institutions focus on profits rather than academic excellence .
With around 2,000 Centres of Legal Education already operating in the country, the focus must shift to consolidation, quality enhancement, and systemic strengthening rather than expansion .
The unchecked mushrooming of institutions has led to widespread academic malpractice and dilution of standards . Previous BCI Measures –
In 2016, the BCI urged State governments and universities to stop approving new law colleges .
The move was aimed at curbing the proliferation of sub-standard institutions and improving the quality of legal education.
However, the advisory did not have the force of law, and many States continued to grant NOCs .
In 2019, the BCI imposed a three-year moratorium on opening new law colleges, citing falling academic standards .
The moratorium was aimed at preventing the commercialisation of legal education and widespread academic malpractice .
However, the moratorium was subsequently set aside by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in December 2020 .
In August 2025, the BCI again announced a three-year nationwide moratorium on the establishment of new law colleges .
The Council stated that with around 2,000 law colleges already in operation, the focus should be on quality enhancement rather than expansion .
During the moratorium, existing colleges were to face intensified inspections and compliance audits, with the power to close down sub-standard institutions .
The 2025 moratorium allowed certain exceptions, including institutions catering exclusively to Socially and Educationally Backward Classes, SC/ST communities, and Economically Weaker Sections .
Proposals for colleges in remote, tribal, or aspirational districts and courses designed for persons with disabilities were also exempted .
However, all such proposals had to satisfy strict conditions, including valid NOCs, prior university affiliations, and demonstrated infrastructure and faculty strength .
In March 2026, the BCI withdrew the August 2025 moratorium and shifted its approach to an inspection-based framework .
Instead of relying on a blanket ban, the Council adopted a framework under which proposals for new law colleges, additional courses, or increased intake are assessed through statutory inspections .
The change came after the moratorium was challenged before the Supreme Court by the Vocational Education Foundation Society . Recent News –
On 23 July 2026, the BCI directed all universities to conduct physical inspections of every affiliated and constituent law college within six weeks .
The move followed oral observations by the Supreme Court during the hearing of a petition regarding the quality of legal education .
The Council said that universities have a primary and continuing responsibility to ensure that affiliated institutions comply with the standards prescribed under the Rules of Legal Education, 2008 .

On 29 July 2026, the Andhra Pradesh High Court in All Saints Christian Education Society v. State of Andhra Pradesh reaffirmed that universities have a continuing duty to ensure that affiliated law colleges comply with the rules of legal education .
The court upheld the disaffiliation of All Saints Christian Law College, which was found running from about 4,762 square feet – a fraction of what its sanctioned intake of 720 students required .
The College had tried to accommodate the extra students by running morning and afternoon shifts, which the BCI had already deemed impermissible .
Following the Andhra Pradesh High Court judgment, the BCI issued a fresh circular on 4 August 2026 .
The circular significantly expands the scope of inspections and mandates that every future affiliation decision must be preceded by a physical inspection .

The BCI warned that affiliation cannot be reduced to a documentary formality and that every student must receive legal education in an institution possessing the prescribed faculty, infrastructure, and academic environment .
Universities have been directed to verify land ownership, classrooms, libraries, moot court halls, legal aid clinics, and sports facilities .
Inspection teams must examine original documents, take geo- tagged photographs, and prepare evidence-based reports .
Generic remarks such as "satisfactory" or "compliant" will not be accepted .
Inspection teams must verify faculty appointments, teacher- student ratios, attendance records, and the actual presence of teachers .
They must examine appointment letters, joining reports, workload, salary payments through banking channels, and compliance with UGC pay norms .
Part-time or visiting faculty cannot replace the mandatory full- time core faculty prescribed under the Rules of Legal Education .
The BCI has directed universities to verify whether institutions have shifted campuses without approval, admitted students beyond the sanctioned intake, or started unapproved courses or sections .
Universities have been instructed not to include any college in counselling, admission, or examination processes unless it possesses valid university affiliation and current BCI approval .
No admissions should be allowed merely because an application for affiliation or approval is pending .
A key focus of the circular is colleges conducting law programmes through morning, evening, weekend, compressed, or overlapping schedules .
The Andhra Pradesh High Court found that such arrangements were not recognised under the regulatory framework .
The BCI has reiterated that a regular law course must involve at least five hours of continuous study every day and a minimum of thirty working hours every week .
Where material deficiencies are detected, universities have been directed to issue show-cause notices and pass reasoned orders after considering the institution's response .
The BCI has cautioned against repeatedly granting conditional affiliation to colleges with fundamental shortcomings .
Cases involving suspension, withdrawal, or refusal of affiliation must be immediately reported to the BCI .
Institutions that fail to comply with the prescribed standards risk regulatory action, including the withdrawal of BCI approval or recognition .
Degrees issued in violation of the Rules may be derecognised, and graduates may be ineligible for enrolment under Section 24 of the Advocates Act, 1961 .
Disciplinary, civil, and criminal proceedings may be initiated against offending institutions and authorities .
The BCI has warned that failure by universities to conduct genuine physical inspections or granting affiliation to sub- standard institutions will be viewed seriously .
Action may be initiated under the Advocates Act, 1961 and the Rules of Legal Education, 2008, including review or withholding of approval .
Universities are also required to appoint a senior nodal officer to coordinate the entire exercise.
